newsitem.title: FRANCE: Alpine peaks claim summer toll among climbers.
newsitem.headline: Alpine peaks claim summer toll among climbers.

text.p: A combination of June snowfalls and August heat has brought a rash of sudden death to the glistening peaks of the Alps.

Almost 100 climbers have died already this summer in the Alps, many of them in the highest and most prestigious range around the 4,807-metre-high (15,869 ft) Mont Blanc, straddling the French-Italian-Swiss borders.

In the treacherous conditions prevailing on the roof of Europe, a climber enjoying the glorious scenery can in seconds become a mangled body crashing down hundreds of metres (feet) amid icy ravines and jagged rocks.
"The past month's climate has created peculiar conditions," said Alberto Re, president of the Italian Association of Alpine Guides.
"Heavy snowfall in June has left a layer of snow which is not compact, and the heat of the past few days has created a lot of dangerous movement."
This summer's grim statistics, while not higher overall than in previous years, show a clear rise in multiple accidents with whole roped parties falling to their death.
Rescuers say these were mostly groups climbing on their own rather than with expensive, professional mountain guides.
Most victims are inexperienced climbers surprised by avalanches and rockfalls triggered by the summer sun or exhausted by trudging through unseasonal, knee-deep snow, experts say.

"The snow cover has been quite heavy for August, which makes it hard for climbing groups to progress," said a gendarme of the French High Mountain Rescue Squad (PGHM). "Many climbers are soon exhausted and then they make mistakes."
Held back by poor weather earlier this summer, thousands of climbers are now flocking to the Alps to escape the August heat down below.
At least 37 climbers have died in France, more than 30 in Italy and at least 25 in Switzerland since the season began little more than a month ago.
"Climbers want to catch up on their plans, come what may, and they go up even in poor mountain conditions," said Eric Bellin, the chief mountain guide in the resort of Chamonix.

Austria's Reinhold Messner, the first man to conquer all of the world's peaks over 8,000 metres (26,400 ft), said amateur climbers saw the Alps as harmless picture postcard mountains rather than the dangerous heights they really are.
"The real problem is that people nowadays don't see them as big, difficult mountains. They don't have respect or fear," he said.
Experts say the death toll has actually lagged behind in relation to the number of climbers flocking to the Alps every summer, probably because rescue operations have increased as well.
Statistics show the death toll on France's mountains as 266 in 1992, 213 in 1994 and 256 last year, while the number of rescue operations grew from 2,835 in 1992 to 3,373 last year.
Rescue operations have improved with the growing use of helicopters, cellular phones and better medical equipment.

Climbers seeing an accident can now call rescuers in seconds, sometimes even while a climber is still falling. Some climbers have called in a rescue helicopter after only a slight accident even though they could have come down on their own.
French taxpayers have to foot the rising rescue bills and critics say imprudent climbers should be charged for calling for help.
The rash of climbing accidents has prompted Messner and others to call for mandatory safety rules.

"It's time for national Alpine associations to organise a European conference to study mistakes made on the mountains and establish new guidelines. Otherwise politicians in Italy France and Switzerland will end up closing he mountains," Messner told the Italian newspaper La Stampa in a recent interview.
Some French officials have suggested a climbing licence.
Top French female climber Chantal Mauduit, who has conquered six 8,000-metre peaks, objected strongly. "Mountains must remain a space for freedom, even if they are hazardous," she said.
